questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Which Harappan site in Gujarat is known for a structure regarded as a dockyard?
questions.explanation: Lothal's large brick basin is generally described as a dockyard.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Which pair of crops is known from Harappan sites?
questions.explanation: Remains of wheat and barley have been found at Harappan sites.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Why are Harappan seals important sources for historians?
options: They carry writing and images that hint at trade and administration
They were coins used throughout the civilisation
They are the only buildings that survive
They record the names of kings in a language we can read
questions.explanation: Seals were used in trade and bear script and motifs, though the script is not read.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Which statement about Harappan houses is correct?
options: All houses were built only of stone
Many houses had bathing areas with drains joined to street drains
Houses had no connection to streets
questions.explanation: Excavated houses show bathrooms and drains linked to street drains.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: What do most historians now say about the decline of Harappan cities?
options: One sudden invasion destroyed every city
Several changes, such as shifting rivers and climate, may have contributed rather than one single cause
questions.explanation: Evidence supports a gradual decline with multiple possible causes.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Granaries have been found at some Harappan sites. What can be inferred?
options: Surplus grain was stored, which suggests organised collection and storage
questions.explanation: Large storage structures suggest surplus and some organisation.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Name any two Harappan sites.
questions.answer: Harappa and Mohenjodaro are two major sites. Others include Lothal, Kalibangan and Dholavira.
questions.explanation: These sites are widely cited in textbooks.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: How do archaeologists use objects like beads and seals to learn about Harappan trade?
questions.answer: Beads made of stones such as carnelian and seals of Indus type found far from their source show that goods moved over long distances. Similar objects at foreign sites suggest contact with other regions.
keyPoints: Objects found far from their source
questions.explanation: The location of objects helps trace trade.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: The Arthashastra, a text on statecraft, is associated with whom?
questions.explanation: Kautilya, a minister of Chandragupta Maurya, is traditionally linked with the text.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Which Chinese pilgrim visited India during the reign of Harshavardhana?
questions.explanation: Hsuan Tsang travelled in India in the seventh century.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why did Ashoka have edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars at public places?
options: To hide them from the people
So that people could read or hear his messages
To mark the graves of kings
questions.explanation: Public inscriptions carried the king's message to his subjects.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why is the Gupta period often called a classical age?
options: The empire was the largest in history
It saw notable achievements in literature, mathematics and art, such as the works of Kalidasa and Aryabhata
questions.explanation: Writers and scholars of the period left a lasting legacy.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why were most of Ashoka's edicts written in Prakrit in the Brahmi script?
options: Ordinary people in much of the empire could understand it
Prakrit was used only by foreigners
questions.explanation: Prakrit was widely understood, so the messages could reach many people.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Which feature best shows that the Mauryan state was centralised?
options: A large salaried bureaucracy and army supported by taxes
Every village governed itself fully with no officials
There were no officials at all
questions.explanation: Paid officials and a standing army show strong central control.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: What was Nalanda in ancient India?
questions.answer: Nalanda was a great Buddhist monastery and centre of learning in Magadha. It attracted students and scholars, including visitors from other countries such as Hsuan Tsang.
questions.explanation: Nalanda is a famous ancient centre of education.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why did Magadha become the most powerful of the Mahajanapadas?
questions.answer: Magadha had fertile land in the Ganga plain, rivers for transport, and nearby iron resources for tools and weapons. Elephants were available for its army, and it had capable rulers.
questions.explanation: Geography and resources supported its expansion.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Who built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
questions.explanation: The Taj Mahal at Agra was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: With which Sufi saint is the dargah at Ajmer associated?
questions.explanation: The Ajmer dargah is linked to Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: For what is Sher Shah Suri remembered?
options: Strengthening the Grand Trunk Road and introducing a silver rupee
questions.explanation: His administration is credited with improved roads and a standard silver coin.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Why is Alberuni's Kitab-ul-Hind valuable to historians?
options: It is a Mughal revenue record
It is an account by a scholar of the eleventh century on Indian society, science and religion
questions.explanation: Alberuni, who came with Mahmud of Ghazni's time, wrote a detailed study of India.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: How did Akbar's policy of treating followers of all religions with respect help his empire?
options: It reduced conflict and helped win the loyalty of a diverse population
It ended the need for an army
questions.explanation: The policy of sulh-i-kul eased tensions among subjects.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: How did the use of Persian as the court language help Mughal administration?
options: A common official language let officials from different regions communicate
It stopped local languages from being spoken
It was spoken only by peasants
questions.explanation: A common administrative language eased governance across regions.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: State two contributions of the Bhakti and Sufi movements to Indian society.
questions.answer: They stressed devotion and the equality of people before God, and used local languages that ordinary people could understand. They also encouraged harmony among communities.
questions.explanation: Both movements reached ordinary people through simple teachings.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Give two reasons for the decline of the Mughal Empire after Aurangzeb.
questions.answer: Long wars, especially in the Deccan, strained the treasury and army, and weak successors fought over succession. Regional powers grew stronger, and invasions such as that of Nadir Shah in 1739 weakened Delhi.
keyPoints: Rise of regional powers or foreign invasion
questions.explanation: Several factors together weakened central power.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Whom did the rebels of 1857 proclaim as their leader in Delhi?
questions.explanation: The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was declared the leader.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: The first railway line in India, opened in 1853, ran between
questions.explanation: The first passenger line connected Bombay and Thane.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Under the Ryotwari system, revenue was settled with
questions.explanation: Revenue was fixed directly with the cultivator, mainly in Madras and Bombay.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: What did Dadabhai Naoroji's drain of wealth theory argue?
options: Britain was investing heavily in India
Wealth flowed from India to Britain without a return
Indian trade was free from duties
questions.explanation: Naoroji argued that part of India's wealth was transferred to Britain.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Why did the British build railways in India?
options: Mainly to carry raw materials to ports and British goods to markets, and also to move troops
To end the need for ports
questions.explanation: Railways served colonial economic and military needs.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Why did the rumour about greased cartridges have such a strong effect on sepoys?
options: It touched their religious feelings, adding to existing grievances
It had no connection with religion
questions.explanation: Rumours of animal fat offended religious beliefs and fed wider discontent.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Name two leaders of the 1857 revolt and the places associated with them.
questions.answer: Rani Lakshmibai led at Jhansi and Nana Sahib at Kanpur. Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow and Tantia Tope are also remembered.
questions.explanation: These leaders are standard examples from the revolt.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Why did the commercialisation of agriculture often leave peasants in debt?
questions.answer: Peasants had to pay revenue in cash and grew crops like cotton and indigo for the market. Price falls or crop failures forced them to borrow from moneylenders, so many fell into debt.
keyPoints: Dependence on market crops and prices
questions.explanation: Market risks and fixed demands pushed peasants into debt.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Which party declared Purna Swaraj as its goal at its Lahore session in 1929?
questions.explanation: The Congress adopted complete independence as its goal at Lahore.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Which movement was launched in 1942 with the call Do or Die?
questions.explanation: Gandhi gave the call at the Quit India session in August 1942.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed the government to
questions.explanation: It permitted detention without trial, so it was widely opposed.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Why did Gandhi link the Khilafat issue with the Non-Cooperation Movement?
options: To unite Hindus and Muslims in a common cause against British rule
questions.explanation: He saw a chance to bring both communities together.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: What was the importance of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931?
options: Civil disobedience was suspended and Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference
questions.explanation: The pact paused the movement and led to Gandhi's attendance in London.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Why did the Quit India Movement spread without a central leadership?
options: It was planned in secret by no one
Major leaders were arrested early, so ordinary people and local leaders carried it forward
The British accepted it at once
questions.explanation: Arrests of the top leaders left local participants to continue.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: What was the significance of the Champaran Satyagraha?
questions.answer: It was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, in support of peasants forced to grow indigo. Its success showed the power of non-violent protest and established Gandhi as a leader.
questions.explanation: Champaran began Gandhi's role in Indian politics.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: How did the national movement become a mass movement under Gandhi?
questions.answer: Gandhi involved peasants, workers and women, not only the educated elite, by using simple symbols such as khadi and salt. His emphasis on non-violence and programmes anyone could join drew wide participation.
keyPoints: Simple symbols like khadi and salt
questions.explanation: Gandhi's methods made participation possible for ordinary people.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Who was elected President of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.explanation: Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Who is popularly called the Iron Man of India for his role in integrating princely states?
questions.explanation: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel played a central role in integration.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: On what main basis were state boundaries redrawn by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956?
questions.explanation: States were reorganised largely along linguistic lines.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Which mission of 1946 came to India to discuss the transfer of power?
questions.explanation: The Cabinet Mission of 1946 proposed a plan for a constitution-making body.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why did the framers choose a parliamentary form of government?
options: They wanted a government accountable to the elected house, and it was familiar from earlier legislatures
They wanted rule by a hereditary monarch
They had never heard of legislatures
questions.explanation: Accountability to the legislature suited the aims of the framers.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why is the Constitution described as partly flexible and partly rigid?
options: It can be amended by any state alone
Some parts can be amended by a simple majority and others need a special majority and state ratification
It has no provisions on amendment
questions.explanation: The amendment procedure differs by provision.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: When was the Constitution adopted by the Constituent Assembly and about how long did the drafting take?
questions.answer: It was adopted on 26 November 1949. The drafting took about two years, eleven months and eighteen days.
questions.explanation: It came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why was Partition in 1947 accompanied by large-scale migration and violence?
questions.answer: Boundaries were drawn on the basis of religious majorities in Punjab and Bengal at great speed, and people feared being a minority on the wrong side. Tension and mistrust led to violence and mass movement across the new border.
keyPoints: Fear and mistrust led to mass migration
questions.explanation: Partition caused one of the largest migrations in history.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Which Article guarantees the right to life and personal liberty?
questions.explanation: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Who appoints the Governor of a state?
questions.explanation: The President appoints the Governor.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Which body conducts elections to Parliament and the state legislatures?
questions.explanation: Article 324 gives this task to the Election Commission.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973?
options: Parliament cannot amend the Constitution at all
The Constitution cannot be changed by anyone
Parliament has no power over taxes
Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure
questions.explanation: The ruling established the basic structure doctrine.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: How long can a Prime Minister continue in office in a parliamentary system?
options: As long as he or she has the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha
As long as the President wishes, whatever Parliament thinks
questions.explanation: The council of ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Why is an independent judiciary considered essential in a democracy?
options: So that courts can obey the executive
So that laws are never questioned
It protects rights and settles disputes impartially, free from control by the executive and legislature
questions.explanation: Independence allows courts to act impartially.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Name the three lists of the Seventh Schedule and give one subject for each.
questions.answer: The Union List includes defence, the State List includes police and public order, and the Concurrent List includes education.
questions.explanation: The lists divide legislative powers between the Centre and states.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: What is a Public Interest Litigation and how has it widened access to justice?
questions.answer: A PIL lets any person or group approach the court on behalf of those who cannot do so themselves, for a public cause. It relaxed the rule that only the affected person could sue, so the poor and disadvantaged gained a path to justice.
questions.explanation: PIL made courts more accessible.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: In which year was the United Nations established?
questions.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 after the Second World War.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Which regional organisation of South Asian countries was formed in 1985?
questions.explanation: SAARC was set up in 1985 at a summit in Dhaka.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: What did the Panchsheel principles of 1954 promote?
questions.explanation: Panchsheel set out principles of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: The Berlin Wall, which fell in 1989, had divided
questions.explanation: The wall separated East Berlin from West Berlin.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why is the veto power of permanent members criticised?
options: It gives all countries a veto
It forces votes in the General Assembly
One permanent member can block a decision even when most members support it
questions.explanation: A single veto prevents action regardless of the majority.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why do neighbouring countries form regional organisations like ASEAN or the EU?
options: To promote economic cooperation and peace through shared rules
To avoid talking to each other
questions.explanation: Shared rules and cooperation reduce conflict and encourage trade.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: What is meant by a bipolar world?
questions.answer: A bipolar world is one in which power is centred in two main states or blocs. During the Cold War the USA and the USSR led rival blocs and most countries were tied to one of them.
questions.explanation: The Cold War world was divided around two superpowers.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Explain how the Cold War shaped the formation of military alliances.
questions.answer: Each superpower sought allies to resist the other, so the USA and its partners formed NATO in 1949, and the USSR and its partners formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The alliances divided Europe into two camps.
questions.explanation: Alliances were a direct product of bloc rivalry.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: What is the term for the movement of people from one place to another to live?
questions.explanation: Migration is the movement of people to live elsewhere.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Which type of rural settlement stretches along a road, river or canal?
questions.explanation: Linear settlements follow a line such as a road or river.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: In the Indian census, a person is counted as literate if aged at least what and able to read and write with understanding?
questions.explanation: The census counts persons aged seven and above who can read and write with understanding.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: In the first stage of the demographic transition, a country typically has
options: low birth and low death rates
low birth and high death rates
high birth and high death rates, with slow growth
questions.explanation: High birth and death rates nearly cancel out.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Why do large cities attract many migrants from rural areas?
options: Cities offer more jobs and better education and health services
questions.explanation: Better opportunities act as a pull factor.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Urban settlements differ from rural settlements mainly because
options: most people work in secondary and tertiary activities rather than farming
questions.explanation: Non-agricultural work is the main feature of urban economies.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Distinguish between natural growth and migration as causes of population change.
questions.answer: Natural growth is the difference between births and deaths. Migration is the movement of people into or out of an area, which also changes the population.
keyPoints: Natural growth equals births minus deaths
Migration is movement in or out
questions.explanation: Population change has these two components.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: How does a rapid fall in death rate with a continued high birth rate affect a country's age structure?
questions.answer: More children survive, so the share of young people rises and the population grows quickly. This increases the dependency ratio and puts pressure on schools, health care and jobs.
questions.explanation: A youthful structure follows when births remain high.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Black soil is regarded as most suitable for which crop?
questions.explanation: Black soil retains moisture and suits cotton.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which of these is a plantation crop?
questions.explanation: Tea is grown on large estates as a plantation crop.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which kind of agriculture is practised on a small plot mainly to feed the farmer's family?
questions.explanation: Subsistence farming mainly supports the farmer's own family.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Why are river valley dams called multipurpose projects?
options: They are built for tourism only
They serve irrigation, power, flood control and water supply together
questions.explanation: One dam provides several benefits at once.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Why do many industries cluster in the same region?
options: Shared infrastructure, labour and markets reduce costs
questions.explanation: Clusters lower costs through shared facilities.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: What is a likely long-term effect of heavy use of chemical fertilisers?
options: Soil may degrade and water may be polluted
questions.explanation: Overuse can harm soil health and pollute water bodies.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: What is rainwater harvesting? State one benefit.
questions.answer: It is the collection and storage of rainwater for later use. It helps to recharge groundwater and provides water in dry periods.
keyPoints: Recharges groundwater or supplies water in dry months
questions.explanation: It reduces dependence on other water sources.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Discuss two environmental problems that mining can cause.
questions.answer: Mining can degrade land by leaving pits and waste heaps, and it can cause deforestation. Waste water may pollute rivers and groundwater, and dust affects air quality.
questions.explanation: Mining affects land, water and air.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Which of these ports is on the Gujarat coast?
questions.explanation: Kandla lies in the Gulf of Kachchh in Gujarat.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: The ancient Silk Route linked
options: China with Europe through West Asia
questions.explanation: It carried silk and other goods between China and the Mediterranean world.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: HDI values lie between
questions.explanation: HDI is expressed on a scale from 0 to 1.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: What does the World Trade Organization mainly deal with?
questions.explanation: The WTO sets and oversees rules for international trade.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: What does the idea of comparative advantage suggest?
options: Countries gain by specialising in goods with lower opportunity cost and trading
questions.explanation: Specialisation and trade can raise output for all partners.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Why is air transport often used for perishable, high-value goods such as cut flowers?
options: It is fast, which keeps such goods fresh, despite the higher cost
questions.explanation: Speed matters most for goods that spoil quickly.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: State two advantages of road transport.
questions.answer: Roads give door-to-door service and are flexible over short and medium distances. They are cheaper to build than railways and can reach remote villages.
questions.explanation: Roads are the most widely used mode for local movement.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: How have information and communication technologies changed trade?
questions.answer: They allow faster exchange of information, so orders and payments can be made quickly. E-commerce widens markets, and global supply chains can be coordinated more easily.
questions.explanation: ICT reduces the cost and time of trade.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: GNP is equal to GDP plus
questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Currency notes in India, apart from small-value ones, are issued by
questions.explanation: The RBI has the right to issue currency notes.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Net national product is gross national product minus
questions.explanation: Depreciation, or capital consumption, is deducted from the gross value.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: When prices keep rising, the purchasing power of money
questions.explanation: Each unit of money buys fewer goods.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: If the marginal propensity to save is 0.25, the marginal propensity to consume is
questions.explanation: MPC + MPS = 1, so MPC = 0.75.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: With a cash reserve ratio of 10 per cent, a fresh deposit of 1,000 can lead to a maximum total deposit of
questions.explanation: Money multiplier = 1/0.10 = 10, so 1,000 x 10 = 10,000.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: What is inflation?
questions.answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level over time. It reduces the purchasing power of money.
keyPoints: Sustained rise in general price level
questions.explanation: Inflation is about general prices, not single goods.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: How does a rise in the repo rate help to control inflation?
questions.answer: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. A rise makes borrowing costlier, so banks charge more for loans, demand for credit falls, and spending and price pressure ease.
keyPoints: Repo rate is RBI's lending rate to banks
questions.explanation: Monetary policy works through the cost of credit.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Under which Article is the annual financial statement, or budget, laid before Parliament?
questions.explanation: Article 112 requires the annual financial statement.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Which of these is an indirect tax?
questions.explanation: GST is charged on goods and services and passed on to the consumer.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Primary deficit equals
questions.explanation: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Which two accounts together make up the balance of payments?
questions.explanation: The balance of payments records current and capital transactions.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: The government borrows to build a new highway. Which measure shows its overall borrowing need?
questions.explanation: Fiscal deficit measures the borrowing the government requires.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Why did India adopt planning after independence?
options: To use limited resources for national development goals, with a major role for the public sector
questions.explanation: Planning aimed to direct resources to development priorities.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: State two features of a mixed economy.
questions.answer: In a mixed economy both the private sector and the public sector exist side by side. The government regulates and provides some goods and services, while private enterprises also produce for profit.
keyPoints: Government regulates and provides some goods
questions.explanation: India follows a mixed economy model.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Explain how globalisation has affected Indian consumers and producers.
questions.answer: Consumers gain more choice and often lower prices because of imports and foreign firms. Producers face more competition and must improve quality, though they also gain access to foreign markets.
questions.explanation: Globalisation brings both opportunities and pressures.
